x-m-h1-01.title: Where did the remainder solution go wrong?
x-m-h1-01.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution that finds a remainder, fix it, and check the wrong answer against the original condition to confirm the error.
x-m-h1-01.material: This is Minjae's solution for finding the constant a so that the remainder is 6 when the polynomial f(x)=x³+ax²+x+2 is divided by x+1. (x³ means x cubed, and ax² means a times x squared.)
x-m-h1-01.thinking.0: Read the whole solution and find the wrong line
x-m-h1-01.thinking.1: Fix the error and find the new answer
x-m-h1-01.thinking.2: Plug the wrong answer into the condition and see the contradiction
x-m-h1-01.prereq.0: You know the relationship between the remainder when a polynomial is divided by a linear expression and the value of the polynomial.
x-m-h1-01.prereq.1: Calculating with expressions that have letters (combining like terms)
x-m-h1-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Minjae's solution that is wrong.
x-m-h1-01.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite x+1 so that the divisor has the form x−(some number).
x-m-h1-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare that number with the value you put into f.
x-m-h1-01.s.s1.line.0: The remainder when f(x)=x³+ax²+x+2 is divided by x+1 is 6.
x-m-h1-01.s.s1.line.1: By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder when dividing by x+1 is f(1).
x-m-h1-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. x+1 can be written as x−(−1), so the remainder is f(−1), not f(1). Lines 3 and 4 just follow line 2, so the calculations inside them are correct, but their results are wrong.
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.prompt: Fix the wrong line and find the value of a. Then also write what the remainder is when you put Minjae's a=2 into f(x) and divide by x+1, to show why Minjae's answer does not work.
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write the value of x that makes x+1=0.
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put the a you found with the corrected line and Minjae's a=2 into f(x), and compare the remainders.
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate f(−1) directly in the corrected solution?
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the remainder when a=2 and show that it is not 6?
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you say how the check reveals the error in the solution?
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.model.0: x+1=x−(−1), so the remainder is f(−1). f(−1)=−1+a−1+2=a, and this is 6, so a=6. If I put in Minjae's a=2, then f(−1)=2, so it is not 6.
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.model.1: When dividing by x+1, I have to put in x=−1, so f(−1)=a. The remainder is 6, so a=6. Check: if a=2, then f(−1)=−1+2−1+2=2, so it does not fit the condition.
x-m-h1-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: Checking with the correct value (if a=6, then f(−1)=6) is also a good method.

x-m-h1-02.title: Make quadratic inequalities with exactly 3 integer solutions
x-m-h1-02.goal: Understand the condition for a quadratic inequality to have exactly 3 integer solutions in terms of the positions of the two roots, then make different examples and check them.
x-m-h1-02.material: There is a quadratic inequality x²+bx+c<0 (x squared plus b x plus c is less than 0). b and c are integers, and you want exactly 3 integers x to satisfy this inequality. Call the two roots α (alpha) and β (beta), from the smaller one.
x-m-h1-02.thinking.0: Turn the condition into the positions of the roots
x-m-h1-02.thinking.1: Think about how the boundary (< versus ≤) matters
x-m-h1-02.thinking.2: Make several examples that satisfy the condition
x-m-h1-02.prereq.0: The relationship between the roots of a quadratic equation and where the graph of the quadratic function meets the x-axis
x-m-h1-02.prereq.1: The difference in meaning between the signs < and ≤
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.prompt: When there are exactly 3 integer solutions, what must always be true about the difference β−α of the two roots?
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think of one inequality whose solutions are 0, 1, 2 and one whose solutions are −1, 0, 1, and sketch where the roots must be for each.
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about where the roots must be so that the integers just outside the integer solutions (for example −1 and 3 when the solutions are 0, 1, 2) are not solutions.
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.r.a: This may be an idea based only on integer roots like (−1, 3). Test whether the roots can also be non-integers.
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.r.b: At the boundary, < and ≤ can switch. Think of the case where the solutions are 0, 1, 2 and the roots are −1 and 3.
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.r.c: This idea puts the 3 integer solutions in the interval between the two roots and considers the possibilities at both ends.
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.r.d: The number of integer solutions and whether the difference of the roots is an integer must be considered separately. Try an inequality like x²−3<0.
x-m-h1-02.s.s1.explain: If consecutive integers n, n+1, n+2 are solutions, then α<n and β>n+2, so β−α>2. Also, n−1 and n+3 are not solutions, so α≥n−1 and β≤n+3, which gives β−α≤4. It can also happen when the roots are not integers, so the difference does not have to be an integer (the solutions of x²−3<0 are −1, 0, 1).
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose integers b and c to make 3 different quadratic inequalities x²+bx+c<0, each with exactly 3 integer solutions.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.hint.0: First expand a quadratic with integer roots, (x−p)(x−q)<0, to get b and c. Count how many integer solutions there are.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.hint.1: Test whether it is also possible when the roots are not integers. Think about how to count the integers between the two roots in that case.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.fail.c1: b and c must be integers.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.ok.c2: There are two different real roots.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.fail.c2: There are no two different real roots (there is no solution, or the solution set is empty).
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of integer solutions is not 3.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.explain: x²−2x−3<0 is (x+1)(x−3)<0, so −1<x<3, and the integer solutions are 0, 1, 2. x²−4x<0 gives 0<x<4, so 1, 2, 3. x²−3<0 gives −√3<x<√3, so −1, 0, 1. x²−x−6<0 has 4 integer solutions, −1, 0, 1, 2, so it does not work.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of your examples whose roots are integers and one whose roots are not, and explain how the way of counting integer solutions is the same and how it is different.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: In the example with integer roots, think about whether the roots themselves are included in the solutions.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: In the example with non-integer roots, recall how you counted the integer solutions.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. In the example with integer roots, ...
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say why the roots themselves are not counted as solutions in the example with integer roots?
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the same method (counting the integers between the two roots) is used even when the roots are not integers?
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you count one by one to check that your example really has 3 integer solutions?
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.model.0: When the roots are integers (−1 and 3), the sign is <, so the roots themselves are not solutions, and I count only 0, 1, 2 between them. When the roots are not integers (−√3 and √3), I do not need to worry about the roots since they are not integers, and I count the integers between the two roots, −1, 0, 1.
x-m-h1-02.s.s2.because.model.1: Counting the integers between the two roots is the same. The difference is that when the roots are integers, I have to check separately that the roots are not included, and when they are not integers, no such check is needed.

x-m-h1-03.title: What do you need to know to say both roots are positive?
x-m-h1-03.goal: Pick out the information that is really needed to conclude that both roots of a quadratic equation are positive real numbers, and use counterexamples to show that only part of it is not enough.
x-m-h1-03.material: There is a quadratic equation x²+bx+c=0 (x squared plus b x plus c equals 0, where b and c are real numbers). You want to state that both roots are positive real numbers (if there is a double root, that root is positive). You can be told some of the information below.
x-m-h1-03.thinking.0: Pick out the needed and unneeded information
x-m-h1-03.thinking.1: Show that a counterexample exists when the information is not enough
x-m-h1-03.thinking.2: Connect the relationships among the conditions (sum, product, real roots)
x-m-h1-03.prereq.0: You know the relationship between the two roots of x²+bx+c=0 and the coefficients b and c.
x-m-h1-03.prereq.1: You know the condition for a quadratic equation to have real roots.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the information that is absolutely necessary to be sure both roots are positive real numbers. (It is enough to know everything that is needed; do not choose what is not needed.)
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.hint.0: First write the signs of the product and the sum of the two roots when both roots are positive.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether, even if you know the signs of the sum and the product, the roots might not be real.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.o.a: b and c are both integers
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.r.a: You can see that being an integer or not has no direct connection to the signs of the roots. For example, x²−3x+1=0 has integer coefficients but non-integer roots.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.o.b: b²−4c ≥ 0 (b squared minus 4c is at least 0)
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.r.b: This shows the idea that you must check the roots are real before you can talk about their signs.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.r.c: This turned the condition that the product of the two roots is positive into information.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.r.d: This turned the condition that the sum of the two roots is positive into information.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.o.e: x=0 is not a root of this equation
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.r.e: This means c is not 0. Think about whether it is already contained in the other information.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.explain: If the two roots are real (discriminant b²−4c≥0), the sum −b is positive, and the product c is positive, then both roots are positive. If the product is positive, the two roots have the same sign, and if the sum is positive, both are positive. Whether b and c are integers is not needed, and that x=0 is not a root is already contained in c>0.
x-m-h1-03.s.s1.acc.0: e follows from c>0 already, so it is not strictly necessary, but it is not contradictory information. You are right that you chose all three needed pieces of information.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.prompt: Show that knowing only two of the needed pieces of information is not enough. Make two quadratic equations whose roots have a positive sum (−b>0) and a positive product (c>0) but are not real (b²−4c<0), and enter b and c.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what sign b must have and what sign c must have.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.hint.1: Keeping those signs, try making b smaller in size or c larger so that b²−4c is negative.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The sum of the two roots, −b, is positive.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The sum of the two roots, −b, is not positive.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The product of the two roots, c, is positive.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The product of the two roots, c, is not positive.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.ok.c3: b²−4c is negative, so there are no real roots.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.fail.c3: b²−4c is not negative, so there are real roots.
x-m-h1-03.s.s2.explain: x²−2x+5=0 has b²−4c=4−20=−16<0, so there are no real roots. If you only look at the signs of the sum and the product, it looks like the positive conditions are met, but if the roots are not real, you cannot say they are positive. b=−6, c=5 (roots 1 and 5) has real roots and breaks the requirement, so it does not work.

x-m-h1-04.title: Three “at least one girl” solutions give different answers
x-m-h1-04.goal: When two solutions to the same problem give different answers, decide which one is right and explain where the wrong solution counts the same case more than once.
x-m-h1-04.material: From 6 students in all, 3 girls (a, b, c) and 3 boys, 2 representatives are chosen, and at least 1 must be a girl. Seojun said, “Choose 1 girl first (3 ways), then choose 1 of the other 5 students (5 ways), so 3×5=15 ways.” Haeun said, “Take the 15 ways of choosing 2 of the 6 students and subtract the 3 ways of choosing only boys, so 12 ways.”
x-m-h1-04.thinking.0: Compare the two solutions and judge which is right
x-m-h1-04.thinking.1: Find the cases that were counted more than once
x-m-h1-04.thinking.2: Explain why it is wrong using specific cases
x-m-h1-04.prereq.0: The sum rule and product rule for counting
x-m-h1-04.prereq.1: The number of ways to choose some of several people when order does not matter
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.prompt: The two answers are different. Which judgment is most appropriate?
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.hint.0: Split into cases by the number of girls and boys, count directly, and compare with the answers of the two solutions.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.o.b: Seojun is right. If you choose 1 girl first, you count every case without missing any, so it is 15 ways.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.r.b: Counting without missing any and counting without overlap must be checked separately. Look at the representatives who are 2 girls.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.o.d: Both are wrong. The answer is the 9 ways of choosing 1 girl and 1 boy.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.r.d: Check that “at least 1” also includes the case where there are 2 girls.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.explain: Of the 15 ways in all, 3 ways choose only boys, so it is 12 ways. Counting directly also gives (1 girl + 1 boy) 3×3=9 ways and (2 girls) 3 ways, which add up to 12 ways. Seojun's method counted each case of choosing 2 girls twice, so 3 extra ways were added.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.prompt: Explain with specific cases why Seojun's 15 ways is 3 more than 12 ways.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.hint.1: In the same way, compare how many times a representative pair of 1 girl and 1 boy is counted.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The case where the representatives are (a, b) ...
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you show that the example you gave (for example, representatives (a, b)) really is counted twice?
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check how many cases are repeated and that this matches the difference of 3?
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you point out that a pair that includes a boy is counted only once?
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.model.0: The cases of choosing 2 girls were counted twice. For example, the pair (a, b) comes up twice: “choose a first and then b” and “choose b first and then a”. There are 3 such pairs, so 3 extra ways were counted.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.model.1: The pairs with two girls are counted twice in Seojun's method. The three pairs (a, b), (a, c), (b, c) are each counted twice, so there are 3 more than the actual 12 ways.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: A pair that includes a boy has only one girl, so it is counted only once.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.hint.1: Following Seojun's method exactly, write out all 15 representatives and look for whether the same representative appears several times.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.o.a: Haeun is right. If you subtract only the cases that don't meet the condition from the total, it is 12.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.r.a: You are checking the validity of the method of subtracting the cases that don't meet the condition from the total.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.o.c: Both are right. If the way of counting differs, the answer can differ too.
x-m-h1-04.s.s1.r.c: You didn't consider that the same problem has one correct answer. Check whether the same cases were counted in the same way.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write out the representatives made by Seojun's method one by one, and count how many times each same representative appears.
x-m-h1-04.s.s2.model.2: In Seojun's method, if the representatives are (a, b), it is counted twice: a first and b later, and b first and a later. (a, c) and (b, c) are duplicates in the same way.

x-m-h1-05.title: Guess the wardrobe from 60 and 72 outfits
x-m-h1-05.goal: Use the product rule backwards from two conditions to work out unknown numbers, and make several cases that satisfy the conditions.
x-m-h1-05.material: Mina's wardrobe has a tops and b bottoms (there are fewer tops than bottoms, a<b), and c hats. The number of outfits where she picks 1 top, 1 bottom, and 1 hat is 60. But if she is allowed not to wear a hat, the number of outfits becomes 72.
x-m-h1-05.thinking.0: Connect the two pieces of evidence to work out the hidden numbers
x-m-h1-05.thinking.1: Find several solutions that satisfy all the conditions
x-m-h1-05.thinking.2: Give the reason you are sure there are no more
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the outfits with a hat and the outfits without a hat do not overlap, so that adding them gives the total.
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.hint.1: Use the fact that an outfit without a hat is made of only a top and a bottom, and write it as an expression in a and b.
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.explain: Outfits without a hat are just choosing a top and a bottom, a×b ways, and this is 72−60=12. Adding these 12 ways to the 60 ways with a hat gives 72 ways.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter at least two different (a, b, c) that satisfy both conditions. (a, b, c are natural numbers and a<b)
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.hint.1: Once the value of a×b is fixed, find the possible pairs a, b among its divisors and check a<b.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, c are natural numbers.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, c must be natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.ok.c2: There are fewer tops than bottoms.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of tops a must be less than the number of bottoms b.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.ok.c3: There are 60 outfits with a hat.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of outfits with a hat is not 60.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.ok.c4: If she does not have to wear a hat, there are 72.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.fail.c4: The number of outfits when she does not have to wear a hat is not 72.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.explain: a×b=12 and c=5. The pairs of natural numbers with a<b are only the three pairs (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4). (4, 3) breaks a<b. (2, 5, 6) gives 60 outfits with a hat, but there are 10 outfits without a hat, so it gives 70.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Write how you found (a, b, c) and why you are sure there are no other cases.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Recall how you checked all the possible pairs after the value of a×b was fixed.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write which pairs the condition a<b removes.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in what order you found a×b=12 and c=5?
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say how the condition a<b filters out something like (4, 3)?
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.model.0: 72−60=12 is the number of outfits without a hat, so a×b=12. Then from 60=12×c, c=5. The pairs with a×b=12 and a<b are only 1×12, 2×6, 3×4. I checked all the divisors of 12, so there are no other cases.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.model.1: a×b=12, so looking for pairs of divisors of 12 gives (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4). These are all the divisor pairs, and c is fixed by 60÷12=5.
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.o.a: The sum of the numbers of kinds of tops and bottoms, a+b
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.r.a: This may be a mix-up of sum and product. The number of outfits is counted by the product.
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.o.b: The number of outfits worn without a hat
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.r.b: This shows the idea of treating not wearing a hat as one of the choices.
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.o.c: The number of kinds of hats, c
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.r.c: If you take 12 to be the number of hats, then 60=12×(a×b), so a×b=5, and you can check whether that fits with 72.
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.o.d: The number of outfits that increases when you buy one more top
x-m-h1-05.s.s1.r.d: If tops increase by one, b×c ways of choosing the new top with a bottom and a hat are added. There is not yet any evidence that this value is 12.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether you can use what you found in the first step to decide the number of hats, c, first.
x-m-h1-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you give the reason that there are no other cases?

x-m-h1-06.title: Why is the expansion formula for (A+B)² different for matrices?
x-m-h1-06.goal: Use a counterexample to show that the commutative law does not hold for matrix multiplication, and explain how this affects the product formulas.
x-m-h1-06.material: For numbers, (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b² always holds. Does (A+B)²=A²+2AB+B² also hold for square matrices A and B of the same size? Here A is the 2×2 matrix whose first row is (1, 1) and second row is (0, 1), and B is the 2×2 matrix whose first row is (p, q) and second row is (r, s).
x-m-h1-06.thinking.0: Decide the condition under which the formula holds
x-m-h1-06.thinking.2: Explain how the counterexample affects the formula
x-m-h1-06.prereq.0: The definitions of addition and multiplication of 2×2 matrices
x-m-h1-06.prereq.1: Expanding expressions with letters (the distributive law)
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.hint.0: Expand (A+B)(A+B) using the distributive law and write down all the terms.
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the expanded expression with A²+2AB+B² and see which terms are different.
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.o.a: It always holds as long as A and B are both 2×2 square matrices
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.r.a: This assumed the multiplication rules for numbers can be used for matrices as they are. Check whether you may change the order in matrix multiplication.
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.o.b: It holds only when A or B is the identity matrix or the zero matrix
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.r.b: Test whether those are the only cases where it holds. For example, think about A and A.
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.explain: (A+B)²=(A+B)(A+B)=A²+AB+BA+B², so for this to equal A²+2AB+B², we need AB+BA=2AB, that is, BA=AB. In matrix multiplication, AB and BA may not be equal.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose integers p, q, r, s (each from −9 to 9) so that AB and BA are not equal. Make two different B.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate each entry of AB and BA directly in terms of p, q, r, s.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the entries in the same positions of the two matrices and find where they differ.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from −9 to 9.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The entries must be integers from −9 to 9.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.ok.c2: AB and BA are different (when you compare the entries they are not equal).
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.fail.c2: AB and BA become equal. Calculate the entries of the products directly and compare them.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.explain: The entries of AB are (p+r, q+s) in the first row and (r, s) in the second row, and the entries of BA are (p, p+q) in the first row and (r, r+s) in the second row. For the two matrices to be equal, we need r=0 and s=p, so if r≠0 or s≠p, then AB≠BA. (p, q, r, s)=(3, 2, 0, 3) makes the two products equal, so it does not work.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one B you made, show one entry where AB and BA differ, and write how this affects the expansion of (A+B)².
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pick one entry where AB and BA differ and write the two values side by side.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write the two middle terms when you expand (A+B)(A+B).
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. When p=1, q=0, r=1, s=1, the AB ...
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you show with numbers a position where the entries of AB and BA differ?
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why AB+BA in (A+B)² cannot be combined into 2AB?
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check your calculation one more time for the B you chose?
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.model.0: If p=1, q=0, r=1, s=1, then row 1, column 1 of AB is p+r=2, but row 1, column 1 of BA is p=1, so they differ. Expanding (A+B)² gives AB+BA, and since AB and BA differ, they cannot be combined into 2AB.
x-m-h1-06.s.s2.because.model.1: The commutative law does not hold, so AB and BA differ. So (A+B)² is A²+AB+BA+B², and it cannot be combined into 2AB. For example, if p=0, q=1, r=1, s=0, then row 2, column 2 of AB is s=0 and row 2, column 2 of BA is r+s=1.
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.o.c: It holds if AB=BA, but there is a B for which it holds even if AB≠BA
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.r.c: You are right up to the point that it holds if AB=BA. But compare what condition is needed for AB+BA and 2AB to be equal in the expanded expression.
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.o.d: It holds when AB=BA, and only then
x-m-h1-06.s.s1.r.d: This shows the thinking of expanding the left side with the distributive law and comparing where it differs from the right side.

x-m-h1-07.title: Will the line touch the circle? When information is revealed one piece at a time
x-m-h1-07.goal: Predict the position of a line and a circle depending on the value of the constant k, revise your judgment with new information, and narrow down the range of k for which they are tangent.
x-m-h1-07.material: There is a circle x²+y²=25 (center at the origin, radius 5) and a line y=x+k. Change the value of k and look at the number of points where the line and the circle meet.
x-m-h1-07.thinking.1: Revise your prediction with new information
x-m-h1-07.thinking.2: Estimate the tangent condition from information
x-m-h1-07.prereq.0: The meaning of the equation of a circle x²+y²=r²
x-m-h1-07.prereq.1: The relationship between the number of solutions when you solve a line and a circle together and the number of intersection points
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.prompt: Each time a value of k is revealed, predict and choose the number of intersection points or the tangent value.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.hint.0: You can check the number of intersection points by the solutions of the equation you get by solving the equations of the line and the circle together.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.hint.1: Also write the method of comparing the distance from the origin to the line with the size of the radius.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.0.info: When k=1, the line is y=x+1. (The y-intercept 1 is less than the radius 5.)
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many points do the line and the circle meet at?
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.0.after: x²+(x+1)²=25 simplifies to x²+x−12=0, so x=−4, 3, and the intersection points are (−4, −3), (3, 4), 2 in all. A line passing through a point inside the circle (near the origin) always meets the circle at two points.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This shows the idea that a line passing through the inside of a circle meets the circle twice.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that the line is outside the circle. Think about how far the origin is from the line.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment that the line is tangent. Think about the fact that the line passes near a point inside the circle, the origin.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.1.info: k was raised to 7. The line y=x+7 meets the y-axis at (0, 7), and 7 is greater than the radius 5.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many intersection points are there?
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.1.after: x²+(x+7)²=25 simplifies to x²+7x+12=0, so x=−3, −4, and the intersection points are (−3, 4), (−4, 3), 2 in all. The distance from the origin to the line x−y+7=0 is 7/√2 (7 over root 2) ≈ 4.95, which is less than the radius 5. Even if the y-intercept is greater than 5, the line is slanted, so it reaches the circle.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.info: When k=7 there were 2 intersection points, and if k is raised to 8, there are no intersection points.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which positive value of k makes the line tangent to the circle?
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.after: When it is tangent, the distance |k|/√2 from the origin to the line x−y+k=0 is 5, so k=5√2≈7.07. Using the discriminant also gives, from 2x²+2kx+k²−25=0, D/4=50−k²=0, so k²=50. At 7.5, D/4=50−56.25<0, so they do not meet.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Compare with the information that there were already 2 intersection points at k=7.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.reflect: At first it seemed that for k=7, where the y-intercept is greater than the radius, they would not meet, but in fact they met at two points. What information made you revise your prediction? What check could you make a habit so that intuition does not mislead you?
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.prompt: For k=7, explain why the first idea “the y-intercept is greater than the radius, so they do not meet” was wrong, using the distance between the origin and the line or the coordinates of the intersection points.
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.hint.0: Recall what feature of the line you left out of your first idea.
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write the equation you get by solving the line and circle together for k=7, and check the solutions.
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If you look only at the y-intercept, ...
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you connect why the y-intercept alone is not enough with how slanted the line is?
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write down the values you calculated (the distance or the intersection points) as numbers?
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you also explain with this method why they do not meet when k=8?
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.model.0: I must not look only at the y-intercept. The line is slanted, and the distance from the origin to the line, 7/√2≈4.95, is less than the radius 5, so they meet. In fact, (−3, 4) and (−4, 3) are the intersection points.
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.model.1: If a line is slanted, it can reach the circle even if the point where it meets the y-axis is outside the circle. Solving them together, x²+7x+12=0 gives x=−3, −4, so they meet at two points.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If you judge by the y-intercept alone, you can miss the effect that the line's slope creates. Consider the distance from the origin to the line.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Whether it is tangent has to be checked by the distance or by the discriminant. You can calculate it.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is the thinking of looking not only at the y-intercept but at how close the line is to the circle. It is a judgment that doubts that intuition and calculation may differ.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It fits the information that the value is between 7 and 8. But calculate whether the distance k/√2 between the origin and the line at this k is greater or less than 5.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Look again at the information that k=7. 6 is less than 7.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment that connects the two pieces of information and uses the fact that the value at which it is tangent lies between 7 and 8.
x-m-h1-07.s.s1.st.2.r.e: It sounds plausible, but check whether the distance between the origin and the line at 7.5 is greater or less than 5.
x-m-h1-07.s.s2.model.2: Solving y=x+7 and x²+y²=25 together gives x²+7x+12=0, so x=-3, -4. So even if the y-intercept is greater than 5, they meet at two points.

x-m-h1-08.title: Find the error in a solution that rearranges the equation of a circle
x-m-h1-08.goal: Find and fix the wrong line in a solution that changes the equation of a circle to standard form, and check the result with a point on the circle.
x-m-h1-08.material: This is Subin's solution for finding the center and radius of the circle x²+y²−4x+6y−12=0. (x² means x squared, and 6y means 6 times y.)
x-m-h1-08.thinking.0: Find the position of the error in the logical flow of the solution
x-m-h1-08.thinking.1: Fix the error and find the center and radius
x-m-h1-08.thinking.2: Check with a point on the circle
x-m-h1-08.prereq.0: The standard form of the equation of a circle (x−a)²+(y−b)²=r²
x-m-h1-08.prereq.1: The meaning of a perfect square expression
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Subin's solution that is wrong.
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.hint.0: Expand (x−2)² and (y+3)² separately and compare them with the left side of the previous line.
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.hint.1: Count which terms newly appear or disappear between the expanded expression and the previous line.
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.line.0: From x²+y²−4x+6y−12=0, group the x terms and the y terms: (x²−4x)+(y²+6y)=12
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.line.1: Turning these into perfect squares gives (x−2)²+(y+3)²=12
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.line.2: So the center is (2, −3) and the radius is √12=2√3.
x-m-h1-08.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. (x−2)²=x²−4x+4 and (y+3)²=y²+6y+9, so to turn the left side into perfect squares we added 4 and 9, which means we must add 4 and 9 to the right side too. Line 3 only reads off the result of line 2, so the way of reading it is correct.
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.prompt: Find the radius with the correct solution, then choose one point on the circle and put it into the original equation to check that the center and radius you found are right.
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.hint.0: The constants newly created on the left must also be added equally to the right side to keep the equation true. Find their sum.
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a point that is moved from the center horizontally or vertically by the radius, and put it into the original equation.
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If you add ... to the right side, ...
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say where the two numbers 4 and 9 that must be added come from?
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the point you chose is the radius away from the center?
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you put that point into the original equation and calculate whether it gives 0?
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.model.0: To make (x−2)² we added 4, and to make (y+3)² we added 9, so we add 4 and 9 to the right side too, 12+4+9=25. So the radius is 5, and the point (2, 2) is 5 above the center, so it is on the circle, and putting it into the original equation gives 4+4−8+12−12=0, which is correct.
x-m-h1-08.s.s2.model.1: While changing to perfect squares, 4 and 9 were newly created, so the right side must be corrected to 12+4+9=25. The radius is 5. As a check, putting in (7, −3) gives 49+9−28−18−12=0, so it is a point on the circle.

x-m-h1-09.title: “If n² is even, then n is even” — which argument is a proof?
x-m-h1-09.goal: Compare checking examples, proving the converse, and proving the contrapositive to decide which shows that the proposition is true, and explain with an example that the original proposition can be false even when its converse is true.
x-m-h1-09.material: Three students tried to show that the proposition “If n² is even, then n is even” about a natural number n is true, and they said the following. Sia: “When n=2, 4, 6, n² is 4, 16, 36 and n is even too, so it is true.” Doyun: “The converse, ‘If n is even, then n² is even,’ is true: let n=2k, then n²=4k²=2(2k²). So the original proposition is true too.” Jihu: “The contrapositive, ‘If n is odd, then n² is odd,’ is true: let n=2k+1, then n²=4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1. So the original proposition is true too.”
x-m-h1-09.thinking.0: Evaluate whether an argument is a proof
x-m-h1-09.thinking.1: Tell apart a proposition, its converse, and its contrapositive
x-m-h1-09.thinking.2: Build and explain the structure of a counterexample
x-m-h1-09.prereq.0: The meaning of the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of a proposition
x-m-h1-09.prereq.1: Writing odd and even numbers with letters (2k, 2k+1)
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.prompt: Which of the three people correctly showed that the original proposition is true?
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.hint.0: First write down how what each student showed is related to the original proposition (original, converse, contrapositive).
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.hint.1: Test with another proposition whether that relation guarantees the truth of the original proposition.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.o.a: Sia. It holds for several even numbers, so it is true.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.r.a: You must distinguish between holding for a few examples and holding for all natural numbers.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.o.b: Doyun. If the converse is true, the original proposition is true too.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.r.b: Check whether a proposition and its converse always have the same truth value. You can make a counterexample.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.o.c: All three showed it correctly. Only the methods differ and the conclusion is the same.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.r.c: You did not check one by one whether the reasons behind the three arguments are all the same kind.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.o.d: Jihu. If the contrapositive is true, the original proposition is true too.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.r.d: This judgment uses the property that a proposition and its contrapositive have the same truth value.
x-m-h1-09.s.s1.explain: A proposition and its contrapositive always have the same truth value, so Jihu's argument, which showed the contrapositive is true for every natural number n, is a proof of the original proposition. Sia checked only some examples, and Doyun only proved the converse. Even if the converse is true, that does not make the original proposition true.
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.prompt: Give another proposition that shows Doyun's reasoning (“the converse is true, so the original proposition is true”) is wrong in general, and write the truth values of the original proposition and its converse.
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.hint.0: Think of a statement of the form “If ..., then ...” similar to the present proposition.
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.hint.1: Find a counterexample that makes the original proposition false, and check that its converse is true.
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The proposition ... is ..., but its converse ... is ...
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you show with a counterexample that the original proposition you gave really is false?
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that its converse really is true?
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that this example shows why Doyun's reasoning is wrong?
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.model.0: The original proposition ‘If it is a rhombus, then it is a square’ is false (a rhombus with an angle that is not 90 degrees is a counterexample). But its converse ‘If it is a square, then it is a rhombus’ is true. So you cannot say the original proposition is true just because the converse is true.
x-m-h1-09.s.s2.model.1: ‘If x²=4, then x=2’ is false because x=−2 is a counterexample. But its converse ‘If x=2, then x²=4’ is true. Even if the converse is true, the original proposition can be false.

x-m-h1-10.title: Is there an inverse function? When the domain and codomain change
x-m-h1-10.goal: Decide whether a function has an inverse function depending on its domain and codomain, then revise your judgment with new information to find the formula and domain of the inverse function.
x-m-h1-10.material: Consider the function f(x)=x²−2x+3. (x² means x squared. This expression can also be written as (x−1)²+2.) The domain and codomain change at each step.
x-m-h1-10.thinking.0: Revise your judgment when the conditions change
x-m-h1-10.thinking.1: Check whether it is a one-to-one correspondence using a counterexample
x-m-h1-10.thinking.2: Check the formula you found with one point
x-m-h1-10.prereq.0: The meaning of the domain, codomain, and range of a function
x-m-h1-10.prereq.1: The meaning of a one-to-one correspondence
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.prompt: Make a judgment each time the domain and codomain change, and revise your judgment when you see new information.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.hint.0: Choose two different values of x and check whether the values of f are the same.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.hint.1: When the domain and codomain change, first check whether the same counterexample is inside the domain.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.info: This is the function f(x)=x²−2x+3, whose domain and codomain are both all real numbers.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: Does f have an inverse function?
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.after: f(0)=3 and f(2)=3, so different values of x have the same value. Then there are two values of x to match with y=3, so the inverse function cannot be defined. This is because it is not a one-to-one correspondence.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It exists. Because it is a function that gives exactly one y value for every x
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is the idea that being a function is enough. Check the case where different values of x have the same value.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It does not exist. Because there are cases where different values of x have the same value
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the idea of finding a case where different inputs have the same output and using it as a counterexample.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It does not exist only at x=1
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is the idea of judging whether an inverse function exists at only one point. Consider whether the whole function is a one-to-one correspondence.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.info: Reduce the domain to {x | x ≥ 1}, and also change the codomain to {y | y ≥ 2}. Now f is a function from {x | x ≥ 1} to {y | y ≥ 2}.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Does this function have an inverse function?
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.after: For x≥1, f(x)=(x−1)²+2 gets larger as x gets larger, so different values of x have different values. Also, the range is all of y≥2, so it is the same as the codomain. So it is a one-to-one correspondence and has an inverse function.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It exists. Because in the domain different values of x do not have the same value, and the range is the same as the codomain
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is an idea that checks the domain and codomain together.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It does not exist. Because f(0)=f(2)=3
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This used the reason from the previous step as it was. Check whether x=0 is in the new domain.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It does not exist. Because the domain and codomain look different
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Even if the domain and the codomain look different, it can still be a one-to-one correspondence. Think again about what conditions are needed.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.2.info: Call the inverse function f⁻¹. f(3)=6.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.2.after: From y=(x−1)²+2 and x≥1, x−1=√(y−2), so x=1+√(y−2). Swapping the variables gives f⁻¹(x)=1+√(x−2), and the domain is x≥2, the range of f. f⁻¹(6)=1+√4=3, which matches f(3)=6. For the other choices, f⁻¹(6) would be −1 or 1, so they are wrong.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The domain must be written as the domain of f⁻¹, not the domain of f. Think about which set of values it has to be.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This choice checks whether f⁻¹(6)=3 using f(3)=6 and also considers the domain.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Substitute and check whether f⁻¹(6) is 3.
x-m-h1-10.s.s1.reflect: Could you use the reason you gave for “does not exist” in the first step again in the second step? What conditions on the domain and codomain must you check for an inverse function to exist, and how did you check them with one point on the formula you found?
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.prompt: Explain what changed between the first step and the second step so that an inverse function exists.
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the counterexample from the first step is also in the domain of the second step.
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how whether the codomain equals the range is related to the existence of an inverse function.
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. By reducing the domain to ..., ...
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say that the counterexample f(0)=f(2)=3 is not in the new domain?
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say what role it plays to make the codomain equal to the range?
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you compare how the reason you wrote differs from the reason in the first step?
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.model.0: By reducing the domain to x≥1, pairs like f(0)=f(2)=3 are no longer both in the domain. I also made the codomain equal to the range, y≥2, so it became a one-to-one correspondence.
x-m-h1-10.s.s2.model.1: If x is at least 1, different values of x always have different values, and by setting the codomain to y≥2 it became equal to the range. So reducing the domain is what gave us the inverse function.
